blocks.text: In the video demo/aks-tutorial: which command created the deployment, when exactly was it run, and what did the terminal show right after?
I'll answer this from the scry index: list the videos, search for the deployment command, then confirm the run and its output with transitions and frames.

lines: **The command** was `kubectl create deployment` for the kodekloudapp image with one replica. Both the OCR and the vision reader agree on this exact text (L1634, frames 202-215; the transition's own reading of the entered text on T198 matches), and I confirmed it by eye on frame 198:
**When it ran.** Enter was pressed at transition T198, between frames 197 and 198.
Command line complete, not yet run                                T197       758.9 s
Enter pressed, command executed (submitted: yes, confidence 0.94) T198       759.4 s (about 12:39)
Output stays on screen, no new input                              frame 198  759.5 to 763.3 s
**What the terminal showed right after.** Two new lines appeared under the command and nothing else (T198 records exactly three changed boxes on frame 198):
The output line is 198:b89 (L1611, both readers agree, visible from 759.5 s for the rest of the session). The fresh empty prompt with a blinking cursor is 198:b91.

scenes.caption: The same agent through the project's MCP server, from Claude Code: 6 tool calls, 52 seconds
scenes.voice: It is also an MCP server, so Claude Code or Copilot can ask the same questions of any indexed video. Ask which command created the deployment: the host lists the videos, searches the index twice, pulls the transitions, and opens the cited frame. The answer gives the exact command, the second it ran, and what the terminal showed next.

scenes.caption: Frame 198, box b89: the cited output line, with the command above it
scenes.voice: Every claim cites a frame and a box: here, frame 198 and box b89, the output line, with the command above it.

scenes.caption: 27 of 27 with the frames open; one rubric line separates the indexes without them
scenes.voice: On a 221-frame sample and 27 questions, every configuration answered everything with the frames in hand. With the frames withheld, the annotated index still answered everything; the unannotated one missed one line, carried by a frame description.

scenes.caption: Second readings collapse between half and forty percent scale; the cost barely moves
scenes.voice: Labels fall off a cliff before the cost does: second readings hold to two-thirds scale and collapse below half, while the cost barely moves. The image scale stays at one.

scenes.caption: $17.85 a video on Opus 5, $12.11 in batch, $4.62 without annotation
scenes.voice: The whole record costs 17 dollars 85 a video on Opus 5, 12 dollars 11 in batch mode, and 4 dollars 62 without annotation. Cheaper models cut the price by half and more, and broke the rule that suggested text is never recorded as typed.

scenes.caption: $0.263 and 22.5 s a question on Opus; the Sonnet agent at a quarter of the price opens far fewer frames
scenes.voice: Answering costs 26 cents and 22 seconds a question on Opus. A Sonnet agent answers at a quarter of the price and ties on score, but opens a fraction of the frames and rarely says when the two readers differ.

scenes.caption: Gemini direct: 17 of 22 questions, 7 of 14 exact strings; the pipeline: 22 of 22, 14 of 14
scenes.voice: Asked directly, Gemini answered 17 of 22 questions and read 7 of 14 exact strings; the pipeline read all 14, and never invented a run.
